snippet.title: Microsoft Outlook Just Went Down. What Actually Broke?
snippet.description:
UPDATE, Nov. 13, 12:57 p.m. ET: Microsoft says the outage was "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents," caused by a problem from an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change. It has addressed the underlying issue and reports broad recovery, while still restoring remaining customers and regions. A full post-incident report is coming.

On Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, many people couldn't reach their mailboxes in Exchange Online, the Microsoft system behind business Outlook. Microsoft also listed Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and Defender XDR as possibly affected. Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports in the U.S. at the peak. Reports are not a count of affected people.

As of this recording (about 3:40 p.m. ET): At 2:07 p.m. ET (admin-center incident EX1550543) Microsoft said it had paused all deployments and configuration changes as a precaution while it reviews recent changes for any link to the outage. At 2:30 p.m. ET it said the elevated load was not driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable. In its 2:58 p.m. ET update (MO1550821; @MSFT365Status, 3:19 p.m. ET), Microsoft said it had not identified any recent changes that correlate with the start of impact, and that the failed health checks "may originate from a specific component on the affected servers." At 3:38 p.m. ET (MO1550821) it said that while validating that change, many affected servers had become unresponsive, and it was restarting them so they come back online with the change in place. That is a working theory, not a confirmed root cause. At 7:06 p.m. ET, Microsoft said servers it had returned to service "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic," and that it was analyzing diagnostic data, temporarily limiting some types of traffic, and rebuilding some servers using a previous software configuration.

#claude #chatgpt #ai #tech #layoff

But what is REALLY happening to tech jobs in 2026?

The tech industry is changing rapidly, and the recent workforce reductions at companies like Oracle and adidas have once again raised a very important question:

👉 Are tech jobs becoming less secure?

Or is something bigger happening behind the headlines?

In this video, we break down the recent Oracle layoffs and adidas India Technology layoffs, what these developments could mean for technology professionals, and why the conversation around AI, automation, restructuring and the future of work is becoming increasingly important.

But this video isn’t just about layoffs.

We’re talking about the bigger picture:

🔹 Why are companies restructuring their technology teams?
🔹 Why can companies invest heavily in AI while reducing certain roles?
🔹 Is AI actually replacing tech jobs — or changing the nature of those jobs?
🔹 What does this mean for software engineers, data engineers, developers and other tech professionals?
🔹 Why are transferable skills becoming increasingly important?
🔹 What skills should technology professionals focus on in 2026?
🔹 How can you become more AI-assisted instead of being afraid of AI?
🔹 Why should you build your professional identity beyond your current employer?
🔹 How can you prepare for career uncertainty BEFORE you actually need to?

💻 THE BIGGEST TAKEAWAY

The question isn’t only:

“Will AI take my job?”

A better question is:

“Which parts of my job are changing, and what skills should I build next?”

Technology will continue to evolve.

Tools will change.

Roles will change.

Companies will restructure.

And the professionals who continuously learn, adapt and understand the bigger business problem will have more skills and options to work with.

Whether you’re a:

✅ Software Engineer
✅ Data Engineer
✅ Data Scientist
✅ Cloud Engineer
✅ Developer
✅ Business Analyst
✅ Tech Lead
✅ IT Professional
✅ Student entering the technology industry
✅ Mid-career professional trying to stay relevant

— this conversation is for you.

🚀 SKILLS TO THINK ABOUT IN 2026

SQL | Python | Cloud | AWS | Azure | GCP | Data Engineering | Spark | Data Warehousing | dbt | AI | AI-assisted development | System Design | Problem Solving | Business Understanding | Communication

You don’t need to learn everything.

Pick a direction. Build depth. Keep adapting.

And most importantly — don’t wait for a layoff email to start thinking about your career.

Build your skills while things are going well.

Build your network before you need it.

Build your portfolio before you need it.

And keep learning before the industry forces you to.

What skill are YOU currently learning to stay relevant in the changing tech industry?

And if you’re currently working in tech, share this video with someone who needs to hear this.

Because here we don’t just talk about getting a job.

We talk about building a career.

snippet.title: Can You Actually Trust Your AI Agent? | Keynote - Munich Tech Winner #haiec #aiassurance HAIEC.com
snippet.description:
HAIEC.com

HAIEC's core architectural commitment is that no large language model participates in its evaluation path. The company's doctrine is "Not AI testing AI." Every finding resolves to source evidence, and evidence that is missing is rendered honestly as unknown rather than inferred.

This deterministic approach means re-running the same evaluation on the same evidence produces the same result. Every conclusion is traceable to a source artifact. Every unresolved question stays visible as a frontier. The output is defensible because the method is defensible.

The platform's evidence store enforces write-once immutability at the database level. Every snapshot is SHA-256 hashed and parent-chained. Every bundle is Merkle-anchored with inclusion proofs. According to HAIEC, even a compromised administrator account cannot alter past evidence.

---

## The Five-Plane Authority Model

At the center of HAIEC's methodology is a five-plane authority model that keeps distinct questions separate rather than collapsing them into a single score:

1. **Requested** — What the AI asked to do
2. **Policy Authorized** — What policy says is allowed
3. **Effectively Granted** — What credentials actually permit
4. **Code Capable** — What the code can reach if invoked
5. **Observed** — What actually happened

Gaps between planes are the findings. The platform never conflates permission with delegation, or code capability with observed action.

A sixth dimension, Delegated Action Integrity (DAI), compares what an agent was delegated to do against what it was code-capable of, what its credentials granted, and what was observed. DAI states include `INSIDE_ESTABLISHED_DELEGATION`, `CAPABILITY_OUTSIDE_DELEGATION_UNMEDIATED`, `OBSERVED_OUTSIDE_DELEGATION`, and `UNRESOLVED_DELEGATION_EXPOSURE`. The last state explicitly captures cases where evidence is missing — because missing evidence is not the same as a violation.

---

## Agent-Operated Assurance

HAIEC exposes its capabilities through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing AI development agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Devin to operate HAIEC directly from the environment where developers work. The production MCP endpoint supports sixteen tools, including `haiec_preflight`, `haiec_run_assurance`, `haiec_get_agent_audit`, and `haiec_runtime_preflight`.

The company's positioning is direct: "Your AI operates HAIEC. HAIEC determines the evidence."

The MCP implementation is intentionally a thin control plane. HAIEC's security invariants include `MCP != ANALYSIS_ENGINE`, `AI_INTERPRETATION != HAIEC_FINDING`, and `AI_PROPOSAL != HUMAN_APPROVAL`. The agent may investigate, interpret, and propose. It may not silently upload evidence or start runtime tests. Those operations require explicit human confirmation.

The platform also supports a zero-account, local developer-security quick check. The AI AppSec package includes 122 detectors and 79 security checks across Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, JSX, and TSX. The MCP Tenant Isolation package includes 57 deterministic rules for detecting cross-tenant failures in multi-tenant SaaS and MCP server code. Both are available without a HAIEC account.

snippet.title: I Worked in Big Tech: Here’s How to Actually Manage Your RSUs
snippet.description:
RSUs are the biggest wealth builder in tech, yet most people don't understand how they're taxed. This video walks through how RSUs work, how they're taxed, and when to sell, in the order it actually happens to you.

Most RSU mistakes come from one misunderstanding: thinking capital gains tax applies to your whole vest. It doesn't. It only applies to the growth after vest. Once you get that, the "hold for a year to save on taxes" logic looks very different.

In this video:
• How a dollar-value grant turns into a number of shares
• Grant date vs. vest date vs. sell date
• Vesting cliffs and schedules (25/25/25/25, Amazon's backloaded schedule, Google's front-loaded one)
• Why 22% withholding often isn't enough, and where the surprise April tax bill comes from
• Short-term vs. long-term capital gains, and why they only touch growth after vest
• 3 selling strategies: sell at vest, sell in chunks, or hold long term
• Why holding to save on taxes can cost more than it saves
